question: Which of these animals lives the LONGEST?

post.premise: A vertebrate that can be born in the 1600s and still be swimming
post.bait: Whale, tortoise or shark — which did you pick? 👇

v04.text: The Greenland shark. A single female was dated at roughly 400 years old.

v05.text: That beats the bowhead whale at 200, and any tortoise. Its age was read in the lens of its eye.

v06.text: It grows about 1 centimetre a year in freezing water, and is not an adult until around 150.

v07.text: So a shark off Greenland today may have been born before the United States existed.

research.topic: Longest-lived vertebrate: the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus). Nielsen et al., Science 2016, dated 28 females by eye-lens radiocarbon: the largest (502 cm) 392 ± 120 years (95.4 % range 272–512), sexual maturity at least 156 ± 22 years, growth about 1 cm a year; bowhead whale can live more than 200 years (NOAA Fisheries); Jonathan the Seychelles giant tortoise is the oldest known living land animal at about 190 (Guinness). Even the low estimate (272 years before 2016 = 1744) predates the United States (1776).

myths.myth: Tortoises are the longest-lived animals with a backbone.
myths.reality: Giant tortoises reach about 190; the bowhead whale passes 200; the Greenland shark was dated to roughly 400 years, with a range of 272 to 512.

landscape.our_gap: Feed clips say 'a 500-year-old shark' over stock footage; nobody shows the age table against whale and tortoise, the 150-year adolescence, or that even the cautious estimate predates 1776 — on a map of where it lives.
